meta.date: ~588 BC (Lehi's death; the psalm written after)

world_behind.title: Blessing over the parents' heads
world_behind.text: To Laman's children Lehi leaves a startling legal transfer: if cursing comes, it will "be answered upon the heads of your parents" (v. 6). Ancient blessing-law let a patriarch redirect liability, and Lehi uses it to fence the grandchildren off from their fathers' account: "the Lord God will not suffer that ye shall perish" (v. 7).

world_behind.title: A death in half a verse
world_behind.text: The man whose sermons filled three chapters gets no deathbed scene: "he waxed old. And it came to pass that he died, and was buried" (v. 12). The record's proportion is deliberate: it spends its metal on what Lehi said, not on grief, and the grief instead breaks out sideways, in the psalm.

world_behind.title: A true Hebrew psalm
world_behind.text: Verses 16–35 run the individual lament's exact form: complaint, remembrance of past mercies, self-exhortation, petition, vow of praise. The family carried Judah's liturgy into exile in someone's memory, and Nephi composes inside the form as one raised on it.

world_behind.title: The soul-track named
world_behind.text: "Upon these I write the things of my soul" (v. 15): the two-records doctrine (1 Ne. 9; 19) restated as the psalm's doorway. The history track got the quarrels; these plates get the interior. What follows is the clearest example in the record of what the small plates are for.

world_behind.title: The credential list
world_behind.text: Support in the wilderness, preservation on the deep, love "unto the consuming of my flesh" (v. 21), night visions, ministering angels, a body carried to "exceedingly high mountains" (v. 25): the remembrance section is Nephi's inner biography, and it matches the outer one the record has told since the valley of Lemuel.

world_behind.title: Jeremiah in the vow
world_behind.text: "Cursed is he that putteth his trust in the arm of flesh" (v. 34) tracks the curse of Lehi's contemporary (Jer. 17:5) nearly clause for clause, including "maketh flesh his arm" (v. 34). The prophet Jerusalem jailed while Lehi fled speaks the psalm's closing doctrine from the brass plates.

words.text: The passive matters: "I, Nephi, was constrained to speak unto them, according to his word" (v. 14). Constraint in this record is the Spirit's pressure on someone who would otherwise stay quiet, and its first appearance was at Laban's body (1 Ne. 4:10). Here it accounts for the anger the preaching keeps producing. What the brothers heard as a younger brother's sharpness, the writer sets down as speech he was not free to withhold.

words.text: "O wretched man that I am" (v. 17): Paul's exact cry (Rom. 7:24), from the record's least wretched man. The word is the psalm's honest opening position, sorrow "because of my flesh" (v. 17), grief for "mine iniquities" (v. 17), and its placement matters: the confession comes from the obedient son. In this record, closeness to God sharpens self-sight.

words.text: To cry out. The verb appears once in this record and never in the King James Bible. Nephi assigns the psalm's sharpest line to a part of himself instead of speaking it flat: "my heart exclaimeth" (v. 17). The device holds through the rest of the verse, where the heart sorroweth and the soul grieveth, each grief given its own organ.

words.text: Surrounded, not merely troubled: "I am encompassed about, because of the temptations and the sins which do so easily beset me" (v. 18). The verb puts the difficulty on every side of the man at once, which is why the petition further down asks for a replacement enclosure rather than an exit: "wilt thou encircle me around in the robe of thy righteousness" (v. 33). Both are wraps. The prayer is about which one is worn on the outside.

phrases.text: The psalm's verb of appetite: delight "in the scriptures" (v. 15), delight "in the things of the Lord" (v. 16). The phrase becomes Nephi's signature; when he introduces Isaiah's chapters later he will sound it again and again (2 Ne. 11). Delight, in his usage, is not mood but orientation: what the soul keeps returning to.

phrases.term: Nevertheless, I know in whom I have trusted
phrases.text: The psalm's hinge, one word wide. Groaning stands on one side, the whole remembrance section on the other, and "nevertheless" (v. 19) carries the turn. Faith in this sentence is not the absence of the groan but the refusal to let the groan finish the sentence.

phrases.text: The father's reveille (2 Ne. 1:13), inherited and turned inward. Lehi shouted awake at sleeping sons; Nephi, weeks later, shouts it at himself. The command's change of address is the farewell cycle's quietest lesson: the sermon you receive becomes the one you must preach to your own soul.

The psalmists' bedrock title (Ps. 89:26), planted at the vow of praise and answered at the close by "the rock of my righteousness" (v. 35): the psalm is framed in rock. Between those two fixed points run all the psalm's motions, weeping, waking, petitioning; the ground under them never moves.

phrases.term: Shake at the appearance of sin
phrases.text: The petition goes past resisting sin to flinching at its silhouette: "Wilt thou make me that I may shake at the appearance of sin" (v. 31) Asked by the man who just catalogued his own besetting temptations, it is a prayer for recalibrated reflexes, holiness as a startle response, built in by request.

phrases.text: Jeremiah's figure for every human substitute for God, sworn off twice in one verse. The psalm's last doctrine is allegiance: trust placed in God "forever" (v. 34), and the curse quoted over the alternative. The record will keep the phrase as its standing term for misplaced reliance (2 Ne. 28:31).

verses.label: v. 3–11
verses.title: The blessings go to grandchildren first
verses.text: The order of the deathbed audience is set out one group at a time and it is not the order a reader expects. Lehi calls "the children of Laman, his sons, and his daughters" (v. 3), then "the sons and daughters of Lemuel" (v. 8), then the sons of Ishmael and all his household (v. 10), then Sam (v. 11). Laman and Lemuel themselves are named in this chapter only as the fathers of the children being addressed and, at verse 13, as men who were angry afterwards. The two eldest sons are present in the chapter and never spoken to in it.

verses.label: v. 6–7
verses.title: A curse redirected to the parents
verses.text: The record preserves a transfer stated in plain terms inside the blessing on Laman's children: "if ye are cursed, behold, I leave my blessing upon you, that the cursing may be taken from you and be answered upon the heads of your parents." Verse 7 draws the conclusion, "because of my blessing the Lord God will not suffer that ye shall perish." A grandfather blesses grandchildren by moving a consequence onto his own sons, and does it while those sons are in the room.

verses.label: v. 12
verses.title: A death in eight words
verses.text: The record ends a man who has occupied most of two books without any ceremony: "he waxed old. And it came to pass that he died, and was buried." No age, no place of burial, no mourners named, no last words beyond the blessings already given. The same verse spends more space on how he had spoken, "according to the feelings of his heart and the Spirit of the Lord which was in him," than on his dying.

verses.label: v. 14–15
verses.title: The writer says which plates this is and why
verses.text: Two verses draw the line between the two records before the psalm begins. Verse 14 points elsewhere for the rest: "a more history part are written upon mine other plates." Verse 15 states what belongs here: "upon these I write the things of my soul, and many of the scriptures which are engraven upon the plates of brass." The twenty verses that follow are the most personal passage in the book, and the record explains, immediately beforehand, that they are on this set of plates by design.

verses.label: v. 17–19
verses.title: The turn, and the word that makes it
verses.text: The passage pivots on a concessive: "Nevertheless, notwithstanding the great goodness of the Lord, in showing me his great and marvelous works, my heart exclaimeth: O wretched man that I am!" Two verses of complaint follow, encompassed by temptations and a heart that "groaneth because of my sins," and then a second nevertheless turns it back: "nevertheless, I know in whom I have trusted." The structure is a reversal inside a reversal, and both hinges are the same word.

verses.label: v. 26–30
verses.title: Questions to himself, then orders to himself
verses.text: The record puts four questions in verses 26 and 27 with no addressee but the speaker: why should my heart weep, why should I yield to sin, why should I give way to temptations, why am I angry. Verse 28 stops asking and starts commanding: "Awake, my soul! No longer droop in sin. Rejoice, O my heart, and give place no more for the enemy of my soul." Verse 29 adds two prohibitions and verse 30 repeats "Rejoice, O my heart." A man issues imperatives to his own soul and heart as though they were separate parties.

verses.label: v. 31–33
verses.title: Eight petitions in three verses
verses.text: Wilt stands eight times here, three in verse 31, one in 32 and four in 33, which places this chapter second among the one hundred and ninety-nine chapters of scripture that use the word, behind Alma 31. The requests are put as questions rather than demands: "wilt thou redeem my soul? Wilt thou deliver me out of the hands of mine enemies? Wilt thou make me that I may shake at the appearance of sin?" The self-commands of the previous verses have become appeals, and the same voice that ordered its own heart to rejoice now asks for everything.

chapter.title: The record's most human page
chapter.text: The passage sits between the death notice at verse 12 and the flight of 2 Nephi 5. Inside it the writer records his own condition in the first person: "O wretched man that I am," "the temptations and the sins which do so easily beset me," and, at verse 27, a question about a specific emotion, "Why am I angry because of mine enemy?" The phrase "so easily beset" stands at Hebrews 12:1. Nothing else in these books has a writer name his own besetting sins and his own anger inside the narrative of his own book.

chapter.title: Murmuring and lament are different instruments
chapter.text: The record's great non-murmurer (1 Ne. 18:16) here groans, weeps, and interrogates himself freely. The distinction it draws is directional: murmuring talks about God to men; the psalm talks to God about everything, including the psalmist. Complaint aimed heavenward is worship.

chapter.title: Honesty is the obedient man's burden
chapter.text: Laman never once calls himself wretched; Nephi does. Self-sight in this record scales with light received, which reverses every expectation about who feels their sins: the psalm's grief is a credential.

chapter.title: Memory defeats mood
chapter.text: The turn at verses 20 and 21 is a list of four things already done: "My God hath been my support," "he hath led me through mine afflictions in the wilderness," "he hath preserved me upon the waters of the great deep," and "He hath filled me with his love." Verse 26 then converts the inventory into an argument by question, "if I have seen so great things... why should my heart weep." Verse 28 gives the two imperatives that follow, "Awake, my soul" and "Rejoice, O my heart." Recollection is used here as the instrument, and nothing new is revealed between the complaint and the resolution.

chapter.title: The besetting sin has a name
chapter.text: Twice the psalm says anger, at enemies with faces (v. 13 supplies them). Its honesty is specific, and the specificity is what makes its comfort usable: generic wretchedness has no cure, but a named temptation can be renounced, "Do not anger again" (v. 29), and prayed against.

cites.quote: Do not anger again

spans.text: Do not anger again

chapter.title: Petition as interrogative
chapter.text: Every request from verse 31 on is a wilt-thou question: reverent about God's freedom, bold about God's character, and checked by the psalm's own clause, ask not amiss. The record's model prayer is a question asked of someone known.

chapter.title: The farewell cycle ends in a song
chapter.text: Four chapters of blessings close with the father buried and the son singing to the rock. No coronation, no succession scene: the record hands authority forward by showing whose soul still knows where to stand. Chapter 5's rupture is one verse of anger away.

applications.title: Keep a soul-track
applications.text: Alongside whatever calendar or journal you keep, write the things of your soul somewhere distinct: what you pondered, what pierced you, what you would engrave. The psalm exists because Nephi kept two records; your interior deserves its own plates.

applications.title: Let the nevertheless in
applications.text: Next time the groan is honest, groan it, and then practice the psalm's grammar: state the trust before the feelings resolve. "Nevertheless, I know in whom I have trusted" is sayable on bad days; that is what it is for.

applications.title: Run the remembrance section
applications.text: When mood argues that God has gone quiet, answer with inventory: list five specific supports, deliverances, or answers on paper before re-litigating the present. The psalm turns on evidence; yours will too.

applications.title: Name the anger
applications.text: Nephi's besetting sin had a face and a household. Name yours as precisely: the person, the trigger, the recurring hour. "Do not anger again" became possible only after "why am I angry" got an honest answer.

applications.title: Borrow one petition whole
applications.text: Take a single line of the psalm's asking, shut the gates of hell before me, robe me, clear my way, and pray it verbatim for a week over one specific struggle. Borrowed prayers carry you to places your own words have stopped reaching.

applications.title: Audit the arms
applications.text: List what you actually leaned on in the last crisis: savings, charm, a person, competence. Renounce none of the tools, but re-rank them under the rock; the curse in the verse is for trust misfiled.

questions.text: If someone read only my "things of the soul," would there be anything to read?
Does closeness to God sharpen or dull my sight of my own sins, and what does that say about the closeness?
What is my sentence after "nevertheless," and can I say it during the groan rather than after?
Which mercies in my own credential list have I never written down anywhere?
What am I angry about right now, and what would the psalm's three questions do to it?
When did I last pray for reflexes, to shake at sin's appearance, and not just for rescue after it?
